lesson.title: Kommen Sie! Kommt!
lesson.subtitle: The formal Sie-command (verb first, Sie after) and the plural ihr-command

hook.title: Three Ways to Order Somebody
hook.content: English commands everybody with one word: come! German refuses. One friend gets Komm!; two friends get Kommt!; a stranger gets Kommen Sie! — and that last one is the strangest, because it is really a statement about 'they': the polite Sie is the old third-person plural, so the command says, in effect, 'let the honored they come.' Verb first, Sie second — it looks like a question with the question mark politely removed, and that is almost exactly its history. English once ran the same split: 'go thou' to one, 'go ye' to many — the King James Bible is full of the plural form. German still lives in that world.

footnotes.title: The Question With the Mark Removed
footnotes.content: Wollen Sie kommen? ('do you want to come?') drops wollen and its question mark: Kommen Sie! The polite command is built on the scaffolding of the polite question — which is why it sounds so courtly.

pattern.title: The Full Command Table
pattern.content: ihr-commands: take the ihr ending -t and nothing else — Kommt! Macht! Trinkt! Esst! (essen keeps its vowel: du isst, ihr esst, command Esst!). The Sie-command: the 3rd-person-plural form, verb FIRST, Sie after — Kommen Sie! Machen Sie! Trinken Sie! Sprechen Sie! The irregular one: sein. Its commands are pure history: Sei! (du), Seid! (ihr), Seien Sie! (formal) — the old *bʰu- root wearing command clothes. And the stem-changers hold their line in all three columns: Iss! Esst! Essen Sie! — Hilf! Helft! Helfen Sie!
pattern.linguist_note: Sei ↔ be: the German command of sein comes from the same Proto-Germanic *bʰu- root as English be (OE bēo!). 'Be good!' and 'Sei gut!' are one command, split by two thousand years of drift.

exercises.prompt: Match each command to the audience it addresses:
exercises.meaning: du, ihr, Sie, and the irregular sein command
exercises.explanation: Bare stem for du, -t for ihr, verb-first + Sie for formal — and sein refuses all three patterns: Sei! Seid! Seien Sie!

exercises.prompt: A waiter invites a customer to drink: '_____ Sie ein Glas Wein!'
exercises.explanation: The Sie-command uses the 3rd-person-plural form, verb first: Trinken Sie! — never Trink Sie.
essen's vowel keeps its e→i shift through the table: du isst, ihr esst — command Esst! The -t ending rides on the shifted stem.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the plural ihr-command with its object: 'Do that!'
exercises.explanation: machen → ihr-command Macht! — the same -t you drilled as the ihr ending, now giving orders.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "Sprechen Sie Deutsch = speak German (formal)"

vocab_hints.note: the polite 'they' — verb first, Sie second

exercises.explanation: Verb first, Sie second: Kommen Sie, Machen Sie, Sprechen Sie — the courtly scaffolding of the polite question, minus the question.
cues: Start with "Sprechen" and anchor "Sie" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Command all three audiences: bare stem (du), -t (ihr), verb-first + Sie (formal) — plus Sei!.

use_example.german: Kommen Sie herein und trinken Sie Tee!

summary.takeaway: Komm! / Kommt! / Kommen Sie! — three audiences, three forms; sein answers only Sei! Seid! Seien Sie!.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: commands in the wild — recipes, dialogues and the register switch, where German drops even the verb's subject.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kommen Sie! Kommt! (Sprechen Sie Deutsch = speak German (formal)):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Sprechen Sie Deutsch" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kommen Sie! Kommt! without relying on short-term echo.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

gegenstand.context_phrase: Ein kleiner Gegenstand liegt auf dem Tisch.
gegenstand.context_translation: A small object lies on the table.
gegenstand.etymology_derivation: Calque of Latin objectum (ob- + jacere → gegen- + Stand = standing against).

cousin.etymology_derivation: From Middle French cousin, Latin consobrinus — the shared Romance source of English cousin. [wiktionary]

bein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bainą — the exact twin of English bone; German means leg. [wiktionary]

erdbeere.context_phrase: Die Erdbeere schmeckt im Sommer süß.
erdbeere.context_translation: The strawberry tastes sweet in summer.
erdbeere.etymology_derivation: Erde (earth) + Beere (berry) — 'earth berry'; the Beere element parallels English berry. [wiktionary]

appetit.context_phrase: Ich habe großen Appetit auf Kuchen.
appetit.context_translation: I have a big appetite for cake.
appetit.etymology_derivation: Appetit — borrowed via Old French from Late Latin appetītus (striving, desire); English appetite is the very same Latin word. [wiktionary]

kissen.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic kussin, an early borrowing of Latin culcita, meaning bolster or quilted cushion; English quilt is a later French loan of the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

brust.context_phrase: Sie hält das Baby an ihrer Brust.
brust.context_translation: She holds the baby to her breast.
brust.etymology_derivation: From Old High German brust, from Proto-West Germanic *brust, from Proto-Germanic *brusts. English breast continues the same Proto-Germanic word. [wiktionary]

krankenwagen.etymology_derivation: Kranken (sick person) plus Wagen (car, wagon — exact twin of English wagon, Proto-Germanic *wagnaz); the sick wagon. English ambulance is French, unrelated. [wiktionary]

operation.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin operatio, a performing, from operari (the root of operieren) — the same Latin word as English operation. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
